l: Troy, The Fall of Troy, BOOK II
s: Troy fears that Achilles will overleap its walls, kill its people, and burn its temples, palaces, and homes. The city gains hope when Memnon arrives with his army, but the battle still brings severe danger and loss.

l: Trojans, The Fall of Troy, BOOK II
s: The Trojans mourn Hector and fear the approaching Achaeans. They welcome Memnon joyfully, arm themselves with his Aethiopians, and join the battle against the Argives.

l: Greeks, The Fall of Troy, BOOK II
s: The Achaeans trust in Achilles and prepare to meet the large force emerging from Troy. They suffer heavy losses when Memnon kills Antilochus and drives them back in panic.

l: Priam, The Fall of Troy, BOOK II
s: Priam urges the Trojans to defend their fatherland from the walls until Memnon arrives. He welcomes Memnon with gifts and a feast, hopes that Memnon will destroy the enemy, and gives him a peerless golden cup.

l: Helen, The Fall of Troy, BOOK II
s: Helen remains in Troy while the city suffers for her sake. The Trojans are too afraid of Paris and Helen to openly support Polydamas's proposal that she and her wealth be returned to the Danaans.

l: Hector, The Fall of Troy, BOOK II
s: Hector is described as Troy's former mighty champion, but Achilles has killed him. Polydamas recalls that Hector did not heed his earlier counsel to remain in the ancient home.

l: the Aethiopians, The Fall of Troy, BOOK II
s: The Aethiopians arrive at Troy with Memnon in a countless host. They fight as the chief warriors on the Trojan side and kill many Danaans.

l: Dawn, The Fall of Troy, BOOK II
s: Dawn is Memnon's mother and is described as the goddess who brings light to the world. She reluctantly climbs heaven's highway at morning, and as the Dawn-queen she turns aside the spears hurled at Memnon.

l: Fates, The Fall of Troy, BOOK II
s: The Fates are described as relentless, even toward the gods. Zeus declares that no prayer can prevent the deaths appointed for the coming battle.

l: the Trojan War, The Fall of Troy, BOOK II
s: The battle begins when the Trojans, Aethiopians, and their allies meet the Achaeans on the plain. Achilles devastates Trojan ranks, while Memnon devastates the Argives, and the fighting produces widespread death among men and horses.

l: Memnon's arrival at Troy, The Fall of Troy, BOOK II
s: Memnon arrives at Troy with a countless host of swarthy Aethiopians after Priam's urgent summons. The Trojans greet him with joy, and Priam welcomes him with gifts, a feast, and hopes that he will save the city.

l: Antilochus, The Fall of Troy, BOOK II
s: Antilochus confronts Memnon after Memnon kills Pheron and Ereuthus. He throws a spear that misses Memnon but kills an Aethiopian comrade, then strikes Memnon with a stone before Memnon pierces him above the breast and kills him.

l: Nestor, The Fall of Troy, BOOK II
s: Nestor witnesses the death of his son Antilochus and is overcome with anguish. He calls on Thrasymedes to help drive Memnon away from Antilochus's corpse, but his age prevents him from fighting Memnon directly.

l: Memnon's army, The Fall of Troy, BOOK II
s: Memnon's army includes countless Aethiopians and warriors from many lands gathered to aid Priam. It pours from Troy like dark clouds, fills the plain, and helps drive the Achaeans back.

l: Antilochus's death, The Fall of Troy, BOOK II
s: Antilochus's death occurs after he confronts Memnon in battle. Memnon pierces him above the breast and through the heart, causing grief among all the Danaans and especially anguish for Nestor.

l: Memnon's slaughter of the Argives, The Fall of Troy, BOOK II
s: Memnon slaughters the Argives after killing Antilochus and drives them toward the Hellespont. He continues killing as the Danaans flee in panic, leaving the plain heaped with dead and stained with their blood.

l: The Fall of Troy, The Fall of Troy, Then to the side of Aeacus' mighty son
s: Nestor tells Achilles that Memnon has slain Antilochus, and Achilles confronts Memnon in battle. The two heroes fight with extraordinary strength until Achilles kills Memnon, whose body is carried away by the winds while his Aethiopian comrades are changed into birds. Eos mourns her son and threatens to withdraw her light, but Zeus's thunder and the Hours bring her back to her daily course. The Trojans and Argives continue grieving amid the slaughter, while Memnon's birds circle and lament around his tomb.

l: Achilles, The Fall of Troy, Then to the side of Aeacus' mighty son
s: Achilles hears from Nestor that Memnon has slain Antilochus and turns from the fighting to confront Memnon. After a long and evenly matched struggle, he pierces Memnon beneath the breast-bone and kills him, then pursues the fleeing Trojans.

l: Memnon, The Fall of Troy, Then to the side of Aeacus' mighty son
s: Memnon has slain Antilochus and taken the armour of the dead. He fights Achilles with great strength, but Achilles eventually pierces him with a sword and kills him; his body is then carried by the winds to the grove beside Aesopus.

l: Nestor, The Fall of Troy, Then to the side of Aeacus' mighty son
s: Nestor comes to Achilles grieving for Antilochus and tells him that Memnon has slain his son. He urges Achilles to help recover the dead and avenge his friend.

l: Antilochus, The Fall of Troy, Then to the side of Aeacus' mighty son
s: Antilochus is identified as Nestor's slain son. Achilles promises to avenge his death by killing Memnon.

l: Thetis, The Fall of Troy, Then to the side of Aeacus' mighty son
s: Thetis is described as the chief of the Nereids and the daughter of Nereus. Memnon insults her as a sea-dwelling goddess, while Achilles recalls that she sheltered Dionysus, received the god-smith after his fall from heaven, and released Zeus from bonds.

l: Dawn, The Fall of Troy, Then to the side of Aeacus' mighty son
s: Eos mourns Memnon after Achilles kills him and covers herself in clouds. She threatens to abandon the light of day and descend into darkness, but Zeus's thunder and the gentle pleadings of the Hours lead her back to her daily course.

l: Zeus, The Fall of Troy, Then to the side of Aeacus' mighty son
s: Zeus loves both Achilles and Memnon and gives each extraordinary strength during their contest. He commands the Fates to stand beside them, and his thunder causes Eos to return to her course.

l: Immortals, The Fall of Troy, Then to the side of Aeacus' mighty son
s: The Gods watch the battle between Achilles and Memnon from above, with some favoring each champion. They see the Fates decide the contest, gather the blood that falls from Memnon's body, and transform it into the river Paphlagoneion.

l: Fates, The Fall of Troy, Then to the side of Aeacus' mighty son
s: The twin Fates appear beside Achilles and Memnon while they fight. One dark Fate casts her shadow over Memnon, while the bright Fate's radiance surrounds Achilles.

l: Trojans, The Fall of Troy, Then to the side of Aeacus' mighty son
s: The Trojans fight beside the Aethiopians against the Argives and suffer heavy losses. After Memnon's death they flee from Achilles and later mourn the loss of their king and host.

l: Argives, The Fall of Troy, Then to the side of Aeacus' mighty son
s: The Argives fight in the battle and many fall beneath Memnon's spear. They later remain in the camp among the dead, grieving for Antilochus even as Achilles is praised.

l: the Aethiopians, The Fall of Troy, Then to the side of Aeacus' mighty son
s: The Aethiopians fight as Memnon's comrades and mourn when their king is killed. Eos changes them into birds that fly around Memnon's barrow, wailing for him.

l: Olympus, The Fall of Troy, Then to the side of Aeacus' mighty son
s: Olympus is described as the place where the Gods observe the contest and where Eos is reluctant to return after Memnon's death. Eos eventually goes back toward Zeus's threshold and resumes her passage through the heavenly gates.

l: Troy, The Fall of Troy, Then to the side of Aeacus' mighty son
s: The ranks of Troy fall before Achilles' hands as he turns toward Memnon. The fighting takes place on the plain near Troy, which is darkened by dust and filled with corpses.

l: Aesopus, The Fall of Troy, Then to the side of Aeacus' mighty son
s: Aesopus is a deep-flowing stream beside a fair grove of the bright-haired Nymphs. The winds set Memnon's corpse down there, and Aesopus's daughters later plant many trees around his barrow.

l: battle between Achilles and Memnon, The Fall of Troy, Then to the side of Aeacus' mighty son
s: The battle begins after Achilles answers Nestor's appeal and faces Memnon. The champions fight with stones, spears, and swords in a long, evenly matched struggle until Achilles kills Memnon.

l: death of Memnon, The Fall of Troy, Then to the side of Aeacus' mighty son
s: Achilles' sword pierces Memnon beneath the breast-bone and passes through his body. Memnon falls into a pool of blood, his comrades flee, and the winds carry away his corpse while Eos and others mourn him.

l: transformation of the Aethiopians into birds, The Fall of Troy, Then to the side of Aeacus' mighty son
s: After Memnon's death, a God gives the souls of his Aethiopian comrades wings and changes them into flying birds. Eos later changes the mourning Aethiopians into birds that circle the barrow of their king.

l: Memnon's birds, The Fall of Troy, Then to the side of Aeacus' mighty son
s: Memnon's birds fly around his tomb with wailing cries and scatter dust onto his grave. They continue their battles around the barrow in memory of Memnon, with victors striking the vanquished dead.

l: Memnon's tomb, The Fall of Troy, Then to the side of Aeacus' mighty son
s: Memnon's tomb stands by Aesopus's stream in a grove planted by the daughters of Aesopus. The transformed birds circle it, mourn their king, and continue their ritual contests around it.

l: war between the Trojans and Argives, The Fall of Troy, Then to the side of Aeacus' mighty son
s: The war is shown as a vast and bloody conflict involving Trojans, Argives, Aethiopians, and the champions Achilles and Memnon. The fighting fills the plain with dust, blood, broken spears, and corpses before continuing after Memnon's death.

l: grief for the dead, The Fall of Troy, Then to the side of Aeacus' mighty son
s: Nestor grieves for Antilochus, Achilles grieves for his fallen friend, and Eos grieves intensely for Memnon. The Trojans, Argives, Aethiopians, Gods, and transformed birds also mourn the dead amid the continuing war.

l: The Fall of Troy, The Fall of Troy, BOOK III
s: After Antilochus is buried, Achilles attacks the Trojans in vengeance and nearly reaches Troy before Apollo strikes him with a concealed shaft. Achilles removes the shaft but weakens and dies near the city, fulfilling the prophecy that he would perish by Apollo's arrows before the Scaean Gates. The Trojans attempt to seize his corpse, but Aias defends it and, aided by Odysseus and other Argives, drives the Trojans back to Troy. Paris is wounded and carried into the city, while Aeneas escapes wounded and the surviving Trojans leave the battlefield strewn with dead.

l: Achilles, The Fall of Troy, BOOK III
s: Achilles arms himself after Antilochus's burial and devastates the Trojan army, pursuing the fleeing soldiers to Troy's walls. Apollo strikes him in the ankle with a concealed shaft; although Achilles removes it and continues fighting, he eventually collapses and dies, after which Aias defends his corpse.

l: Antilochus, The Fall of Troy, BOOK III
s: Antilochus's corpse is carried to the ships by the Pylians and buried beside the Hellespont. His death causes Achilles to seek terrible vengeance against the Trojans.

l: Thetis, The Fall of Troy, BOOK III
s: Thetis had told Achilles that he was destined to die before the Scaean Gates by Apollo's shafts. Hera recalls that the gods once prayed that Thetis would bear such a son to Peleus.

l: Apollo, The Fall of Troy, BOOK III
s: Apollo descends from Olympus to stop Achilles after Achilles has slain countless Trojan warriors. He hides himself in cloud and shoots a baleful shaft into Achilles' ankle, causing the hero's fatal weakness.

l: Hector, The Fall of Troy, BOOK III
s: Hector is described as mightier in war-craft than Glaucus, though he had previously shrunk before Aias's spear. Paris also hopes that dragging Achilles's corpse to Troy would bring glory to Hector's horses and to Hector in Hades.

l: Paris, The Fall of Troy, BOOK III
s: Paris urges the Trojans to fight for the chance to drag Achilles's corpse into Troy. He shoots at Aias, but Aias strikes him with a stone, and Paris is carried wounded into Troy by Hector's steeds.

l: Aias, The Fall of Troy, BOOK III
s: Aias stands over Achilles' corpse and prevents the Trojans from carrying it away. He kills many attackers, wounds Aeneas, drives Paris from the field, and forces the surviving Trojans back through Troy's gates.

l: Odysseus, The Fall of Troy, BOOK III
s: Odysseus fights beside Aias during the battle around Achilles' corpse. He kills several Trojans and continues fighting despite a wound near his right knee.

l: Argives, The Fall of Troy, BOOK III
s: The Argives mourn Antilochus and later fight fiercely to defend Achilles' corpse. They kill many Trojans with their spears and leave the dead unstripped until Achilles can be placed on the pyre.

l: Trojans, The Fall of Troy, BOOK III
s: The Trojans initially advance despite their fear of Achilles, but Achilles' attack sends them into panic. After Achilles falls, they attempt to seize his corpse, then flee from Aias and retreat behind Troy's gates.

l: Fates, The Fall of Troy, BOOK III
s: The Fates fill the Trojans with courage while also determining that many will descend to Hades. They have decreed that Achilles will die on the same day as many of the warriors he kills.

l: Troy, The Fall of Troy, BOOK III
s: Troy is nearly breached when Achilles pursues the fleeing Trojans and threatens to destroy the city. Its gates shelter the routed Trojans, Paris, and the wounded survivors after Aias drives them from the battlefield.

l: Scaean Gates, The Fall of Troy, BOOK III
s: The Scaean Gates are identified as the place before which Achilles was destined to die by Apollo's shafts. Achilles's death in this unit fulfills that prophecy near Troy's walls.

l: Achilles' death, The Fall of Troy, BOOK III
s: Achilles' death comes through Apollo's concealed shaft, which wounds his ankle and drains his strength. He continues killing after the wound but finally falls among the dead, terrifying the Trojans even after he is dead.

l: battle for Achilles' corpse, The Fall of Troy, BOOK III
s: The Trojans, led among others by Glaucus, Aeneas, and Agenor, fight to drag Achilles' corpse into Troy. Aias, joined by Odysseus and other Argives, kills many defenders and preserves the corpse for burial.

l: Achilles' corpse, The Fall of Troy, BOOK III
s: Achilles' corpse becomes the object of a fierce struggle between the Trojans and the Argives. Aias guards it, and the Argives eventually retain it, intending to place it on the pyre.

l: vengeance, The Fall of Troy, BOOK III
s: Achilles's vengeance for Antilochus drives his assault on the Trojans and causes widespread slaughter. After Achilles falls, the Trojans seek vengeance by trying to carry his corpse away, but Aias and the Argives prevent them.

l: The Fall of Troy, The Fall of Troy, So the kings drew him from that stricken field
s: Achilles is mourned by the Achaeans after being slain by a god's arrow, and his body is washed, dressed, displayed, and lamented by warriors, captives, Thetis, the Daughters of Nereus, and the Muses. Aias, Phoenix, Agamemnon, and Briseis each grieve for Achilles while recalling his strength, kindness, family, or protection. The Achaeans burn Achilles with lavish offerings, gather his bones in a golden vase, and raise a barrow beside the Hellespont. Poseidon tells Thetis that Achilles will not remain among the dead but will become a god on an island in the Euxine Sea, while Achilles' immortal horses wait for Neoptolemus.

l: Achilles, The Fall of Troy, So the kings drew him from that stricken field
s: Achilles, also called Peleus' son and Aeacus' son, lies dead after being struck by a god's arrow. The Achaeans mourn him for many days, burn his body with rich offerings, preserve his bones, and raise a barrow beside the Hellespont. Poseidon declares that Achilles will rise to the light of Zeus and become a god on an island in the Euxine Sea.

l: Aias, The Fall of Troy, So the kings drew him from that stricken field
s: Aias mourns Achilles, his father's brother's son, and says that no mortal man struck him. He blames the shaft as a weapon used by weakling dastards and fears that Achilles' death will leave the Achaeans vulnerable to the Trojans.

l: Phoenix, The Fall of Troy, So the kings drew him from that stricken field
s: Phoenix mourns Achilles as the child whom Peleus entrusted to his care. He recalls holding Achilles as a baby and hoping that Achilles would support him in old age, then grieves that both he and Peleus must live with sorrow for his death.

l: Agamemnon, The Fall of Troy, So the kings drew him from that stricken field
s: Agamemnon mourns Achilles as the chiefest of the Danaans and says that the Achaean host is now fenceless. He complains that Zeus promised the destruction of Priam's city but has left him unable to attain the war's goal after Achilles' death.

l: Nestor, The Fall of Troy, So the kings drew him from that stricken field
s: Nestor, son of Neleus, advises Agamemnon to end the lament for the day and order the care of the dead. He helps direct the washing, dressing, and laying out of Achilles' body.

l: Thetis, The Fall of Troy, So the kings drew him from that stricken field
s: Thetis mourns Achilles beside the Nereids and later casts herself upon his body. She complains to Zeus that he made Achilles glorious but gave him only a brief life, and she intends to remind Zeus of her suffering and accuse him of failing her son.

l: Briseis, The Fall of Troy, So the kings drew him from that stricken field
s: Briseis tears and beats her breast over Achilles, calling him her sunlight, sweet life, hope, and protection. She says that he treated her like a wife rather than a captive, and she fears being taken by a new Achaean master after his death. She lays her shorn hair on his corpse as her final gift.

l: Peleus, The Fall of Troy, So the kings drew him from that stricken field
s: Peleus is described as Achilles' aged father, who is expected to suffer overwhelming grief when news of Achilles' death reaches him. Phoenix remembers that Peleus welcomed him and entrusted the infant Achilles to his care.

l: Zeus, The Fall of Troy, So the kings drew him from that stricken field
s: Zeus fills the Argive men with courage so they can behold the gathered goddesses, and he rains ambrosia on Achilles' body during the funeral preparations. At Thetis' lament, Calliope warns her not to provoke Zeus, and Poseidon later says that Achilles will rise to the light of Zeus.

l: Neoptolemus, The Fall of Troy, So the kings drew him from that stricken field
s: Neoptolemus, Achilles' fleet-foot son, is expected to come from Scyros to the war-host. Achilles' immortal horses remain by the ships until he arrives, and the Fates have allotted him the horses after Achilles.

l: Nereids, The Fall of Troy, So the kings drew him from that stricken field
s: The Daughters of Nereus hear the Achaeans' mourning and rise from the sea in dark mantles to join the lament for their sister Thetis' son. They shed ambrosia and precious nards over Achilles' bones after the funeral fire.

l: Muses, The Fall of Troy, So the kings drew him from that stricken field
s: The Muses come from Helicon, burdened with grief and honoring the Nereid. They join the divine lament for Achilles, and Calliope tells Thetis that minstrels will preserve Achilles' glory and might through the inspiration of the Muses.

l: Myrmidons, The Fall of Troy, So the kings drew him from that stricken field
s: The Myrmidons mourn Achilles continuously and surround his body. They cut their hair, help prepare and burn the pyre, quench the embers with wine, gather his bones, and place them in a silver casket.

l: Achaeans, The Fall of Troy, So the kings drew him from that stricken field
s: The Achaeans grieve bitterly over Achilles' death, fearing that the Trojans will now defeat them. They wash and dress his body, lament him for many days, conduct his funeral with extensive offerings, and raise a barrow over his remains.

l: Trojans, The Fall of Troy, So the kings drew him from that stricken field
s: The Trojans rejoice at Achilles' fall because they had feared him as sheep fear a lion. Their sons, horses, and other offerings are placed on Achilles' funeral pyre, and Priam's seed is said to have cause for gladness.

l: Immortals, The Fall of Troy, So the kings drew him from that stricken field
s: The gods are said to grant no perfect happiness to mortals, and even sons of Zeus can perish under evil fate. They cannot restrain Fate's power, though divine beings attend Achilles' mourning and funeral.

l: Troy, The Fall of Troy, So the kings drew him from that stricken field
s: Troy is the foemen's land where Achilles lies dead and where the Achaeans fear defeat after his fall. Agamemnon had expected Priam's burg to be destroyed, but doubts that the war's goal can now be won.

l: Hellespont, The Fall of Troy, So the kings drew him from that stricken field
s: The Hellespont is where the Achaean ships lie and where the mourning for Achilles resounds. Achilles' barrow is raised beside its deep waters.

l: Euxine Sea, The Fall of Troy, So the kings drew him from that stricken field
s: The Euxine Sea contains the holy island that Poseidon promises to give Achilles. There Achilles is to become a god whom the surrounding tribes will honor with incense and sacrifice.

l: Achaean fleet, The Fall of Troy, So the kings drew him from that stricken field
s: The ships stand beside the Hellespont while the Achaeans mourn Achilles. Their tents and vessels are drenched by tears, and the mourning host later returns to them after the funeral.

l: Achilles' corpse, The Fall of Troy, So the kings drew him from that stricken field
s: Achilles' body is washed of blood, dressed in sea-purple clothing, and laid on a couch. Athena preserves it with ambrosia and makes it appear like a living, sleeping warrior before it is burned on the pyre.

l: Achilles' bones, The Fall of Troy, So the kings drew him from that stricken field
s: After the pyre consumes Achilles, his bones remain distinct from the other remains. The Myrmidons gather them, place them in a silver casket, and then put the casket in a golden vase over which the Nereids pour ambrosia and nard.

l: Achilles' immortal horses, The Fall of Troy, So the kings drew him from that stricken field
s: Achilles' immortal horses mourn their slain king and long to leave the mortal men and Argive horses. The gods keep them beside the ships until Neoptolemus arrives, after which they are destined to serve him.

l: death-rites of Achilles, The Fall of Troy, So the kings drew him from that stricken field
s: Achilles' funeral includes a vast pyre, battle gear, slain Trojan men, horses, cattle, sheep, captive women's mantles, gold, amber, oils, honey, wine, and perfumes. The winds summoned by Hermes fan the fire, and the Achaeans later gather the bones and build a great barrow beside the Hellespont.

l: Achilles' death and mourning, The Fall of Troy, So the kings drew him from that stricken field
s: Mourning for Achilles spreads through the Achaean host, the Myrmidons, Briseis and the captive women, Thetis and the Nereids, and the Muses. The lament lasts for many days and is compared to the cries of a city destroyed in battle and to the roar of sea-waves.

l: Achilles' death, The Fall of Troy, So the kings drew him from that stricken field
s: Achilles' death is caused by a god's arrow that strikes him unexpectedly rather than in direct combat. His death causes the Achaeans to fear defeat, gives joy to the Trojans, and brings grief to Peleus, Phoenix, Thetis, Briseis, and his companions.

l: Trojan War, The Fall of Troy, So the kings drew him from that stricken field
s: The Trojan War continues after Achilles' death, but Agamemnon fears that the Achaeans can no longer achieve its goal. The Trojans are expected to press their attack toward the ships now that Achilles, the Achaeans' chief strength, has fallen.

l: Fate, The Fall of Troy, So the kings drew him from that stricken field
s: Fate is described as an irresistible power hovering over all mortals and as something that even the gods cannot restrain. The Fates have also assigned the course of Achilles' immortal horses and the later service of Neoptolemus.

l: Achilles' deification, The Fall of Troy, So the kings drew him from that stricken field
s: Achilles' deification is promised by Poseidon, who says that Achilles will not remain among the dead but will rise to the light of Zeus. He will dwell as a god on a holy island in the Euxine Sea and receive incense and sacrificial honors from the surrounding tribes.

l: The Fall of Troy, The Fall of Troy, BOOK IV
s: After Achilles’ death, the Argives mourn beside their ships while the Trojans rejoice, though some Trojans fear the surviving Achaean champions. Zeus foresees Troy’s eventual destruction despite Hera’s reproach, and the Argives prepare to honor Achilles with funeral games. Thetis arrives from the sea, sets out athlete prizes, and oversees contests including a footrace, wrestling, and boxing. Aias of the Locrians wins the footrace, Aias son of Telamon defeats Diomedes in wrestling, and Epeius and Acamas fight to a draw before accepting silver bowls as prizes.

l: Achilles, The Fall of Troy, BOOK IV
s: Achilles is mourned by the Argives, who yearn for him as for a son. His deeds and victories are celebrated by Nestor, and Thetis establishes funeral games and prizes in his honor.

l: Thetis, The Fall of Troy, BOOK IV
s: Thetis comes forth from the sea to the Argives and sets down prizes for Achilles’ funeral games. She rewards the competitors, giving four handmaids to Aias son of Telamon and Diomedes, and presenting silver bowls to Acamas and Epeius.

l: Argives, The Fall of Troy, BOOK IV
s: The Argives mourn Achilles beside their ships, but they eat, sleep, and rise prepared to fight the Trojans. They remain by the ships to await Thetis and participate in or watch the funeral games.

l: Trojans, The Fall of Troy, BOOK IV
s: The Trojans rejoice when they see Achilles’ funeral fire and hope his death will give them relief from war. A prudent Trojan warns that the surviving Achaean champions, including Aias, Diomedes, and the Atreus’ sons, still threaten them.

l: Funeral games of Achilles, The Fall of Troy, BOOK IV
s: The funeral games are held after Thetis arrives with prizes for the Argive champions. They include a footrace, wrestling, boxing, and other athletic contests, with competitors receiving cattle, horses, handmaids, chariots, or silver bowls.

l: Zeus, The Fall of Troy, BOOK IV
s: Zeus is reproached by Hera for helping Troy despite his connection to Peleus and Thetis’ marriage. He remains silent while thinking that the Argives will soon destroy Priam’s city and that he will later bring ruin upon the victors by war and sea.

l: Aias, The Fall of Troy, BOOK IV
s: Aias son of Telamon argues that the Argives should remain by the ships until Thetis arrives. He competes against Diomedes in wrestling, throws him to the ground in the second fall, and then receives four handmaids from Thetis.

l: Diomedes, The Fall of Troy, BOOK IV
s: Diomedes urges the Argives to fight the Trojans despite Achilles’ death, but agrees to await Thetis and the funeral games. He wrestles Aias son of Telamon, throwing him in the first fall before being thrown in the second, after which Nestor stops the contest; he receives two of Thetis’ four handmaids.

l: Nestor, The Fall of Troy, BOOK IV
s: Nestor sings of Thetis, Peleus’ wedding, the deeds of Achilles, and Achilles’ victories. He gives the horses awarded to him to his comrades, and later stops the wrestling contest between Aias son of Telamon and Diomedes.

l: Teucer, The Fall of Troy, BOOK IV
s: Teucer competes in the footrace against Aias of the Locrians. Near the finish, an unearthly power causes his foot to strike a tamarisk root, wrenching his ankle and allowing Aias of the Locrians to win.

l: Aias of the Locrians, The Fall of Troy, BOOK IV
s: Aias of the Locrians races against Teucer and wins after Teucer injures his ankle. His Locrian followers cheer him and lead the cattle he has won to the ships.

l: Idomeneus, The Fall of Troy, BOOK IV
s: Idomeneus rises for the boxing contest, but no one comes forward to challenge him because of his age and standing. Thetis gives him a chariot and swift horses, which he entrusts to his drivers.

l: Epeius, The Fall of Troy, BOOK IV
s: Epeius comes forward for the boxing contest and fights Acamas with bull-hide gauntlets. He and Acamas exchange severe blows until the Argives stop the fight, and Epeius receives one of the two silver bowls from Thetis.

l: Acamas, The Fall of Troy, BOOK IV
s: Acamas challenges Epeius in boxing and uses fighting craft to evade and counter his blows. He is knocked down but rises and continues until the Argives halt the contest; he receives the other silver bowl.

l: Troy, The Fall of Troy, BOOK IV
s: Troy celebrates Achilles’ death, believing that the Achaeans may flee and that the city may gain relief from war. Zeus nevertheless thinks that the Argives will soon destroy the city of Priam.

l: athlete prizes, The Fall of Troy, BOOK IV
s: The athlete prizes are set out by Thetis for Achilles’ funeral games. They include kine and calves for the footrace, horses and a chariot, four handmaids, and two silver bowls.

l: footrace, The Fall of Troy, BOOK IV
s: The footrace is contested by Teucer and Aias of the Locrians. Teucer’s foot is injured by a tamarisk root near the finish, so Aias of the Locrians passes him and wins.

l: Achilles' death and mourning, The Fall of Troy, BOOK IV
s: The Argives mourn Achilles beside the ships, with no eye in the host tearless, while the Trojans rejoice at the sight of his funeral fire. Despite their grief, the Argives eat and sleep before preparing for battle and honoring him with games.

l: Trojan War, The Fall of Troy, BOOK IV
s: The Trojan War continues after Achilles’ death, since the Argives prepare to attack and the Trojans remain concerned about the surviving champions. Zeus foresees the destruction of Troy and later ruin for the victors by war and the sea.

l: The Fall of Troy, The Fall of Troy, Then for the archery-test Oileus' son
s: At Achilles' funeral-feast, athletic contests continue, including archery, throwing the iron bar, leaping, javelin-casting, wrestling, chariot racing, and horse racing. Aias wins the iron-bar contest and receives the arms of Memnon, while Teucer wins the archery-test and receives the arms of Troilus. Agamemnon wins the chariot race, and Sthenelus's horse wins the horse race after swerving from the course. Thetis distributes many prizes, while the Argives celebrate the competitors and Laertes grieves that his wound prevents him from competing.

l: Aias, The Fall of Troy, Then for the archery-test Oileus' son
s: Aias shoots first in the archery-test and strikes the ridge of the helm. He alone hurls the massive iron bar, then challenges the strongest hero to a contest of hands and feet, which no one dares to accept; Thetis gives him the arms of Memnon.

l: Teucer, The Fall of Troy, Then for the archery-test Oileus' son
s: Teucer competes with Aias in the archery-test and shears the plume from the helm with his arrow. The people praise his accuracy despite the pain that makes his foot halt, and he receives the arms of Troilus from Thetis.

l: Agamemnon, The Fall of Troy, Then for the archery-test Oileus' son
s: Agamemnon sets up the helm for the archery-test and declares that the master-shot will shear away its hair-crest. He wins the chariot race through skill and receives a silver-wrought breastplate that belonged to Polydorus.

l: Thetis, The Fall of Troy, Then for the archery-test Oileus' son
s: Thetis distributes prizes throughout the athletic contests. She gives Teucer the arms of Troilus, Aias the arms of Memnon, Agapenor the battle-gear of Cycnus, Euryalus a silver oil-flask, Menelaus a golden cup, and other prizes to the racers; Aias's stature makes her think of her dear son, and she sighs.

l: Achilles, The Fall of Troy, Then for the archery-test Oileus' son
s: Achilles killed Troilus, Cycnus, Mynes, and Memnon, and he spoiled Lyrnessus and Thebes. His swift ships carried the iron bar to Troy, where it served as a reminder of his father and as a test of strength; the contests are held for prizes at his funeral-feast.

l: Menelaus, The Fall of Troy, Then for the archery-test Oileus' son
s: Menelaus competes in the chariot race and wins it by skill, despite having slower horses than those he had previously driven from Elis. He receives a golden cup, once the chief possession of Eetion, from Thetis.

l: Eumelus, The Fall of Troy, Then for the archery-test Oileus' son
s: Eumelus enters the chariot race and leads at the start with his horses. He is later among those whose wounds Podaleirius treats after they fall from their cars.

l: Argives, The Fall of Troy, Then for the archery-test Oileus' son
s: The Argives praise Teucer's archery, marvel at Aias's throw of the iron bar, and shout during the athletic contests. They gaze in wonder at the arms of Memnon and acclaim Agamemnon's victory in the chariot race.

l: Troy, The Fall of Troy, Then for the archery-test Oileus' son
s: Troy is associated with the prizes and deeds remembered in the contests. Achilles killed Troilus and Cycnus there, spoiled its places and peoples, and fought its Trojans while carrying the iron bar as a reminder of his father.

l: archery-test, The Fall of Troy, Then for the archery-test Oileus' son
s: In the archery-test, Aias strikes the ridge of a plumed helm, while Teucer shears away its plume. Teucer is declared worthy of praise for his accurate shot despite his painful foot.

l: athletic contests, The Fall of Troy, Then for the archery-test Oileus' son
s: The athletic contests include archery, throwing the iron bar, leaping, javelin-casting, fighting with hands and feet, chariot racing, and horse racing. Thetis awards arms, armor, cups, vessels, weapons, and other prizes to the competitors.

l: chariot race, The Fall of Troy, Then for the archery-test Oileus' son
s: Menelaus, Eurypylus, Eumelus, Thoas, and Polypoetes compete in the chariot race. Eumelus leads at first, but Menelaus wins through skill; Thoas and Eurypylus are wounded when they fall from their cars.

l: horse race, The Fall of Troy, Then for the archery-test Oileus' son
s: In the horse race, Sthenelus's swift horse takes the lead but repeatedly swerves from the course. The horse still wins second place after Agamemnon outraces it, and its noble lineage from Arion is recounted.

l: Funeral games of Achilles, The Fall of Troy, Then for the archery-test Oileus' son
s: The athletic contests take place at Achilles' funeral-feast. Competitors strive for the prizes that Thetis distributes, while Laertes is prevented from competing by a wound received in the fight around Achilles' dead body.

l: iron bar, The Fall of Troy, Then for the archery-test Oileus' son
s: The iron bar is so heavy that no Argive except Aias can hurl it, and two men can scarcely lift it. It once belonged to Antaeus, was taken by Hercules and given to Peleus, and then passed to Achilles before Aias throws it far.

l: arms of Memnon, The Fall of Troy, Then for the archery-test Oileus' son
s: Thetis gives the arms of Memnon to Aias after he wins the iron-bar contest. The Argives marvel at the giant's war-gear, and Aias alone is considered large and strong enough to wear it.

l: chariots, The Fall of Troy, Then for the archery-test Oileus' son
s: The competitors line their chariots up at the starting-line and drive them across the plain. The chariots seem to fly without leaving wheel-tracks, while dust rises around them; several racers later fall from their cars.

l: horses, The Fall of Troy, Then for the archery-test Oileus' son
s: The horses strain at their harnesses, paw the sand, foam at the mouth, and race across the plain under the drivers' whips and reins. Sthenelus's horse is exceptionally swift and descends from Arion, but its unfamiliarity with the course causes it to swerve.

l: The Fall of Troy, The Fall of Troy, BOOK V
s: Thetis presents Achilles' immortal arms as a prize for the Argive warrior who rescued Achilles' body. Aias and Odysseus claim the arms, but Trojan captives judge Odysseus the victor after the two heroes argue over their battlefield deeds. Aias is overwhelmed by grief and madness, imagining vengeance against the Argives and Odysseus before Athena turns his fury aside. In his madness, Aias attacks and kills sheep, mistaking them for his enemies, until Athena removes the delusion from his mind.

l: Achilles, The Fall of Troy, BOOK V
s: Achilles is dead, and his immortal arms are awarded after contests held in his honor. Aias and Odysseus dispute who did more to rescue his body, with each claiming superior service in battle.

l: Thetis, The Fall of Troy, BOOK V
s: Thetis lays Achilles' divinely wrought arms before the Argives and offers them to the mightiest warrior who rescued Achilles' dead body. She later plunges into the sea with the Nereids, grieving for Achilles.

l: Achilles' armor, The Fall of Troy, BOOK V
s: Achilles' immortal arms include the shield, helmet, corslet, greaves, sword, and spear. The arms become the prize in a rivalry between Aias and Odysseus, and the Trojans award them to Odysseus.

l: shield of Achilles, The Fall of Troy, BOOK V
s: The shield of Achilles is shown as a marvel wrought by Hephaestus, depicting heaven, earth, sea, warfare, peace, agriculture, festivals, gods, ships, and the surrounding Ocean. Its scenes appear so lifelike that the portrayed creatures and people seem to move.

l: Aias, The Fall of Troy, BOOK V
s: Aias, described as the mightiest of the Danaan warriors, claims Achilles' arms because he says he bore Achilles' body from the battle and defended the ships. After the judgment gives the arms to Odysseus, Aias is seized by grief, anger, and madness.

l: Odysseus, The Fall of Troy, BOOK V
s: Odysseus argues that wit, speech, and his own battlefield deeds make him worthy of Achilles' arms. The Trojan captives judge him the victor, and Athena protects him from Aias' intended attack.

l: Argives, The Fall of Troy, BOOK V
s: The Argives assemble for the contest over Achilles' arms, but their leaders refuse to judge the dispute themselves because they fear angering either hero. They groan when Odysseus wins, and Aias' madness threatens their ships and lives.

l: Trojans, The Fall of Troy, BOOK V
s: Trojan captives are appointed to judge which warrior was most feared by the Trojans and who rescued Achilles' body. They unanimously award victory and Achilles' arms to Odysseus.

l: the contest for Achilles' arms, The Fall of Troy, BOOK V
s: Nestor proposes that Trojan captives judge the dispute because they would hate both Greek warriors equally. The captives unanimously give the victory and Achilles' immortal arms to Odysseus rather than Aias.

l: Aias' madness, The Fall of Troy, BOOK V
s: After losing the judgment, Aias becomes violently deranged and plans to burn the ships and kill the Argives and Odysseus. Athena causes him to mistake sheep for his human enemies, and later removes the madness from his mind.

l: Aias's suicide, The Fall of Troy, BOOK V
s: Aias' death does not occur in this unit. After the judgment, Doom follows him, but the passage ends with Athena removing his madness after he has slaughtered sheep.

l: Athena, The Fall of Troy, BOOK V
s: Athena favors Odysseus because of his continual sacrifices to her. She strikes Aias with madness, turns his violence away from the Argive men, and later tears the delusion from his mind.

l: war, The Fall of Troy, BOOK V
s: The shield depicts the horrors of war, including battles, slain men, panic, dread, strife, avenging spirits, and the Fates. The dispute over Achilles' arms centers on the warriors' deeds during the war against Troy.

l: Aias' slaughter of the sheep, The Fall of Troy, BOOK V
s: While mad, Aias attacks and kills sheep, believing that he is striking down the Danaans. He stands over a slaughtered ram and mocks it as though it were Odysseus before Athena removes the madness from him.

l: The Fall of Troy, The Fall of Troy, Then Aias saw those sheep upon the earth
s: Aias realizes that the gods deceived his senses and made him slaughter sheep instead of his enemies, and he kills himself with Hector's sword. Teucer, Tecmessa, and the Danaans mourn him, while Agamemnon promises protection for Tecmessa and her son. Odysseus regrets his quarrel with Aias and attributes the disaster to wrath and fate. The Argives burn Aias's body, gather his bones in a golden casket, and bury them in a great mound near Rhoeteium.

l: Aias, The Fall of Troy, Then Aias saw those sheep upon the earth
s: Aias discovers that the gods have cheated his senses and caused him to slaughter innocent sheep. He curses Odysseus, Agamemnon, and the Argive host for denying him the honor he deserves, then kills himself by thrusting Hector's sword through his throat. The Danaans burn his body, gather his bones, and bury them near Rhoeteium.

l: Teucer, The Fall of Troy, Then Aias saw those sheep upon the earth
s: Teucer embraces Aias after his death and considers killing himself, but the others restrain him. He mourns Aias as his mighty-souled brother and says that he has no desire to return home without him. Agamemnon invokes Teucer's continued life when promising protection to Tecmessa and her son.

l: Tecmessa, The Fall of Troy, Then Aias saw those sheep upon the earth
s: Tecmessa, Aias's captive bride and household-queen, falls upon his corpse and laments his suicide. She grieves that Aias will never return with her and their son to Salamis, and fears that their child will become a wretched thrall and that she will again face bondage. Agamemnon promises that neither she nor her son will be enslaved while Teucer or Agamemnon lives.

l: Odysseus, The Fall of Troy, Then Aias saw those sheep upon the earth
s: Odysseus mourns Aias and speaks with remorse to the Argives. He says that wrath led Aias to his death and wishes that he had never won the contest for Achilles' arms. He attributes Aias's destruction to fate and says that a wise person should endure misfortune steadfastly rather than become its fool through passion.

l: Achaeans, The Fall of Troy, Then Aias saw those sheep upon the earth
s: The Danaans initially watch Aias from a distance in fear, then rush to his body, cast dust upon their heads, and raise a great lament. They carry him to the ships, wash and shroud his body, and collect wood and offerings for his pyre. After the cremation, they gather his bones, place them in a golden casket, and raise a great mound for him.

l: Aias's suicide, The Fall of Troy, Then Aias saw those sheep upon the earth
s: Aias's suicide follows his realization that the gods made him mistake sheep for his enemies and his despair over lost honor. He uses Hector's sword to kill himself, leaving Teucer, Tecmessa, and the Danaans in profound grief. Odysseus connects the act with Aias's wrath, passion, and the working of fate.

l: Aias's funeral, The Fall of Troy, Then Aias saw those sheep upon the earth
s: Aias's funeral includes washing and shrouding his body, placing it upon a large pyre, and surrounding it with wood, animals, clothing, gold, armor, silver, ivory, oil, and other offerings. A wind sent by Thetis drives the fire until his body is consumed. The Danaans quench the pyre with wine, place his bones in a golden casket, and bury them in a high mound near Rhoeteium.

l: wrath, The Fall of Troy, Then Aias saw those sheep upon the earth
s: Wrath is described by Odysseus as a great curse that grows into strife and produces bitter consequences. It drives Aias's rage against Odysseus and contributes to his suicide. Odysseus says that the wise should endure their lot steadfastly rather than become fools of passion.

l: Honour, The Fall of Troy, Then Aias saw those sheep upon the earth
s: Aias believes that the brave no longer receive their due honor while baser men, especially Odysseus, are favored among the Greeks. Odysseus says that honor was the goal of his rivalry with Aias over Achilles' arms, since it is the proper object of competition among right-hearted men. After Aias's death, the Danaans honor him with offerings, cremation, a golden casket, and a great burial mound.

l: The Fall of Troy, The Fall of Troy, BOOK VI
s: Menelaus tests the Achaean men by proposing that they flee Troy, but Tydeides rejects the counsel and Calchas urges that Achilles' son be brought from Scyros. Odysseus and Tydeides sail toward Scyros, while Eurypylus, grandson of Hercules and leader of a host from the Caicus region, arrives to aid Troy. Eurypylus leads the Trojans into battle and kills Nireus and Machaon, after which the Argives fight to recover their bodies.

l: Eurypylus, The Fall of Troy, BOOK VI
s: Eurypylus, the son of Telephus and grandson of Hercules, arrives at Troy with a great host from the region of the Caicus. He is welcomed by Paris and Hector, promises to defend Troy, and leads the Trojan forces in battle. He kills Nireus and Machaon, though Machaon foretells that Eurypylus will soon die on the plain of Troy.

l: Hercules, The Fall of Troy, BOOK VI
s: Hercules is identified as Eurypylus's grandfather. Eurypylus bears a shield depicting Hercules' great labours, and Zeus grants Eurypylus extraordinary strength as a favour to Hercules.

l: Achilles, The Fall of Troy, BOOK VI
s: Achilles is dead. His death causes the Achaeans to seek his son as a source of strength and possible victory.

l: Neoptolemus, The Fall of Troy, BOOK VI
s: Achilles' son is living on Scyros and is described as war-fain and valorous. The Achaeans decide to send Odysseus and Tydeides to persuade him to come and aid them.

l: Menelaus, The Fall of Troy, BOOK VI
s: Menelaus summons the Achaean men and proposes flight from Troy, claiming that continued war will bring further destruction. He secretly desires to destroy Troy and kill Paris, and he promises Hermione in marriage to Achilles' son if the young hero comes to aid the Argives.

l: Tydeides, The Fall of Troy, BOOK VI
s: Tydeides rebukes Menelaus's proposal to flee and calls the Achaeans to prepare for battle. He agrees to accompany Odysseus to Scyros, and later fights among the Achaeans against Eurypylus and the Trojans.

l: Diomedes, The Fall of Troy, BOOK VI
s: Diomedes is mentioned only in the account worked upon Eurypylus's shield, where Hercules is shown killing Diomedes' man-eating horses and their lord.

l: Odysseus, The Fall of Troy, BOOK VI
s: Odysseus supports the plan to bring Achilles' son from Scyros and agrees to undertake the mission with Tydeides. The two men draw a ship into the sea, provision it, and sail toward Scyros.

l: Paris, The Fall of Troy, BOOK VI
s: Paris rejects the prospect of abandoning the war and welcomes Eurypylus to Troy. He urges Eurypylus to defend Troy and later leads him into the city, where Eurypylus is received by Helen.

l: Helen, The Fall of Troy, BOOK VI
s: Helen is blamed by Menelaus for the war and for abandoning their home and marriage-bed. She is described as goddess-like in beauty and marvels at Eurypylus when he is brought to Paris's palace.

l: Nireus, The Fall of Troy, BOOK VI
s: Nireus, famed for beauty, is killed in battle when Eurypylus's spear pierces him beneath the ribs. Eurypylus taunts him and tries to strip his arms, but the Argives later fight to recover his body.

l: Machaon, The Fall of Troy, BOOK VI
s: Machaon attacks Eurypylus in anger over Nireus's death and wounds him in the shoulder. Eurypylus wounds Machaon in the haunch and then kills him by driving a spear through his breast. Machaon foretells Eurypylus's imminent death before his spirit passes into Hades.

l: Greeks, The Fall of Troy, BOOK VI
s: The Achaean men gather at Menelaus's summons and reject the suggestion of flight after Tydeides's rebuke. They prepare their weapons, send Odysseus and Tydeides toward Scyros, and fight the Trojans in a fierce battle.

l: Trojans, The Fall of Troy, BOOK VI
s: The Trojans arm themselves and pray for relief from slaughter before Eurypylus arrives with reinforcements. They welcome Eurypylus, follow him into battle, and initially drive the Argives back under his leadership.

l: Troy, The Fall of Troy, BOOK VI
s: Troy is the city defended by Eurypylus and the Trojans. Paris believes Eurypylus may prevent Troy's destruction, while the Achaeans continue preparing to break its walls.

l: Scyros, The Fall of Troy, BOOK VI
s: Scyros is the overseas place where Achilles' son resides. Odysseus and Tydeides sail toward it to persuade him to join the war.

l: Trojan War, The Fall of Troy, BOOK VI
s: The war continues despite Menelaus's proposal that the Achaeans flee. Eurypylus's arrival intensifies the conflict, producing a major battle in which Nireus and Machaon are killed.

l: journey to Scyros, The Fall of Troy, BOOK VI
s: The journey to Scyros begins when Odysseus and Tydeides provision a swift ship and sail from the Achaean camp. Their purpose is to bring Achilles' son to the war.

l: arrival of Eurypylus, The Fall of Troy, BOOK VI
s: Eurypylus arrives at Troy with a large force of battle-skilled men from the lands along the Caicus. Paris and Hector honour him, and the Trojans rejoice because they expect him to strengthen their defence.

l: death of Machaon, The Fall of Troy, BOOK VI
s: Machaon dies in battle after attacking Eurypylus in revenge for Nireus. Eurypylus pierces him through the breast, and the Argives call on their forces to prevent the Trojans from carrying away his body.

l: death of Nireus, The Fall of Troy, BOOK VI
s: Nireus dies when Eurypylus stabs him beneath the ribs. Eurypylus mocks his beauty and attempts to strip his arms, prompting Machaon to attack.

l: death, The Fall of Troy, BOOK VI
s: Death strikes many warriors in the battle, including Nireus and Machaon. The fighting leaves the earth red with blood, and both sides struggle over the fallen.

l: The Fall of Troy, The Fall of Troy, By this to Podaleirius tidings came
s: Podaleirius learns that his brother has been struck down and leaves his healing work beside the ships to fight, killing Cleitus and Lassus. The Danaans rescue Machaon and Aglaia's son but suffer heavy losses before Eurypylus drives them back toward the ships. Aias, the Atreidae, and other leaders resist until reinforcements rally, but Eurypylus renews the Trojan assault and causes a widespread flight. The Trojans would have burned the ships if night had not intervened, and both sides withdraw after a day of severe slaughter.

l: Podaleirius, The Fall of Troy, By this to Podaleirius tidings came
s: Podaleirius receives news that his brother has been struck down while he is ministering to wounded men beside the ships. He arms himself in anger, enters the battle, and kills Cleitus and Lassus.

l: Machaon, The Fall of Troy, By this to Podaleirius tidings came
s: Machaon is one of the warriors over whom the Danaans fight. The Danaans rescue him and Aglaia's son and carry them toward the ships, though many who attempt the rescue remain surrounded by the battle.

l: Greeks, The Fall of Troy, By this to Podaleirius tidings came
s: The Danaans rescue Machaon and Aglaia's son but suffer many losses in the fighting. Eurypylus drives many of them toward the ships, and they later flee in panic until other warriors rally around Aias and the Atreidae.

l: Argives, The Fall of Troy, By this to Podaleirius tidings came
s: Many Argives flee to the ships under pressure from Eurypylus. They suffer heavy casualties, and their dead are left heaped together on the battlefield.

l: Trojans, The Fall of Troy, By this to Podaleirius tidings came
s: The Trojans press the Danaans hard, killing many and pursuing them toward the ships. They camp exultantly near the outfall of the Simois after night prevents them from burning the ships.

l: Eurypylus, The Fall of Troy, By this to Podaleirius tidings came
s: Eurypylus turns from chasing the Danaans and attacks the Atreus' sons and Oileus' seed. He rallies the Trojans, drives the Danaans into panic, and kills Bucolion, Nesus, Chromion, Antiphus, and many unnamed men before withdrawing with the Trojans.

l: Aias, The Fall of Troy, By this to Podaleirius tidings came
s: Aias is struck on the helmet by a huge stone hurled by Aeneas and is dashed to the ground, but he does not die. His men rescue him from the enemy and carry him, scarcely breathing, to the Achaean ships.

l: Atreus' sons, The Fall of Troy, By this to Podaleirius tidings came
s: The Atreus' sons are nearly left alone amid enemies who surround and attack them from every side. They hold their ground and kill foes, then receive help from Teucer, Idomeneus, Thoas, Meriones, and Thrasymedes before Eurypylus again drives the Danaans back.

l: Paris, The Fall of Troy, By this to Podaleirius tidings came
s: Paris charges beside Iris and Aeneas. Thoas wounds him in the right thigh, after which he retreats toward his bow; he later kills Phorcys, Mosynus, and Cleolaus with arrows and wounds Eetion through the jaw.

l: Aeneas, The Fall of Troy, By this to Podaleirius tidings came
s: Aeneas hurls a huge stone that strikes Aias' helmet and knocks him down, though Aias survives. Aeneas later kills Antimachus and Pheres, who had come from Crete with Idomeneus.

l: Achaean fleet, The Fall of Troy, By this to Podaleirius tidings came
s: The ships are the refuge toward which many wounded and fleeing Danaans are carried or driven. The Trojans approach closely enough that they might have burned the ships, but night forces them to withdraw.

l: Trojan War, The Fall of Troy, By this to Podaleirius tidings came
s: The battle centers first on the struggle over Machaon and Aglaia's son, then expands into a fierce assault and counterassault around the ships. It produces widespread slaughter, panic, wounds, and retreats before night ends the fighting.

l: death, The Fall of Troy, By this to Podaleirius tidings came
s: Death takes many warriors in the fighting, including Cleitus, Lassus, Laophoon, Echemmon, and numerous unnamed men. The dead are left amid blood and agony, while Aias survives despite being knocked down.

l: flight of the Danaans, The Fall of Troy, By this to Podaleirius tidings came
s: The Danaans and Argives flee toward the ships when Eurypylus causes panic in their ranks. The Trojans pursue them like hounds chasing deer and kill many during the retreat.

l: burning of the ships, The Fall of Troy, By this to Podaleirius tidings came
s: The Trojans would have burned the ships after driving the Danaans back. Night, described as trailing heavy-folded mist, rises before they can do so and makes Eurypylus withdraw.

l: The Fall of Troy, The Fall of Troy, BOOK VII
s: After Machaon and Nireus are buried, Eurypylus leads the Ceteians and Trojans in a devastating assault that drives the Argives behind the ships. Odysseus and Diomede travel to Scyros and persuade Achilles' son to come to Troy by promising him Achilles' armor, gifts, and a royal marriage. Deidameia grieves and warns her son against the war, while he insists that he must follow his destiny and win glory worthy of Achilles. Achilles' son finally leaves Scyros with Odysseus, Diomede, and twenty attendants, amid prayers for his safe return.

l: Achilles, The Fall of Troy, BOOK VII
s: Achilles is remembered as a mighty hero and a son of a Goddess who was slain in battle through the wiles and counsels of the men who now seek to bring his son to the war. His son resembles him in form, face, prowess, and eagerness for battle.

l: Neoptolemus, The Fall of Troy, BOOK VII
s: Achilles' son is found at his palace on Scyros practising with dart and lance and driving his chariot. He agrees to sail to Troy when summoned by the Achaean oracles, despite his mother's grief, and leaves Scyros with Odysseus, Diomede, and twenty trusted attendants.

l: Deidameia, The Fall of Troy, BOOK VII
s: Deidameia is grief-wasted by Achilles' death and fears that her son will also perish in war. She pleads with him to remain in Scyros, but after he departs she mourns over his bed, childhood toys, and belongings.

l: Odysseus, The Fall of Troy, BOOK VII
s: Odysseus travels to Scyros with Diomede to bring Achilles' son to the war. He identifies himself as a friend of Achilles, promises to give Achilles' armor to his son, and accompanies him when he leaves for the ship.

l: Diomedes, The Fall of Troy, BOOK VII
s: Diomede travels with Odysseus to Scyros to summon Achilles' son. He is identified as Tydeus' son and goes with Odysseus and the young prince to the ship.

l: Eurypylus, The Fall of Troy, BOOK VII
s: Eurypylus fights with immense strength and kills many Argives, including Peneleos. He drives the Argives behind the rampart of the ships and continues to press the war after the agreed burial truce.

l: Argives, The Fall of Troy, BOOK VII
s: The Argives march out to fight Eurypylus while some remain to bury Machaon and Nireus. Eurypylus overwhelms them, and they flee behind the ships until Athena gives them courage to defend the rampart with darts.

l: Trojans, The Fall of Troy, BOOK VII
s: The Trojans fight alongside the Ceteians against the Greeks and later bury their own dead during the temporary cessation of battle.

l: Scyros, The Fall of Troy, BOOK VII
s: Scyros is the sea-ringed island where Achilles' son lives with Deidameia and Lycomedes. Odysseus and Diomede come there to recruit him, and he eventually departs from the island for the war.

l: Troy, The Fall of Troy, BOOK VII
s: Troy is described as the fount of tears and the place where many, including skilled warriors, perish in battle. Achilles' son is persuaded to go there to help bring the war to an end.

l: Trojan War, The Fall of Troy, BOOK VII
s: The war rages around the ships and the walls, with Ceteians, Trojans, and Greeks suffering heavy losses. Achilles' son chooses to join it so that he may aid the Danaans and perform deeds worthy of his father.

l: the bringing of Achilles' son to Troy, The Fall of Troy, BOOK VII
s: Odysseus and Diomede bring Achilles' son from Scyros by offering him honor, Achilles' armor, gifts, and the possibility of marriage to Menelaus' daughter. His departure is delayed briefly by Deidameia's pleading, but he ultimately sails with them and twenty household attendants.

l: grief for the dead, The Fall of Troy, BOOK VII
s: The Greeks mourn Machaon, Nireus, and Peneleos, while Podaleirius nearly takes his own life beside Machaon's tomb. Deidameia's grief over Achilles and fear for her son are likewise overwhelming, and she continues mourning after his departure.

l: Fate, The Fall of Troy, BOOK VII
s: Fate is said to assign bereavement to all people and to distribute good and evil unpredictably. Achilles' son maintains that no one dies in war beyond destiny and accepts that he should die if his fate is to serve his country.

l: death, The Fall of Troy, BOOK VII
s: Death takes Machaon, Nireus, Peneleos, Achilles, and many other warriors in the fighting. Nestor teaches that all mortals share one path toward death and that the living must endure the grief sent by the Gods.

l: Achilles' armor, The Fall of Troy, BOOK VII
s: Achilles' armor is described as godlike battle-gear fashioned by Hephaestus, with gold worked over a shield depicting earth, heaven, sea, and living creatures. Odysseus promises to give it to Achilles' son when he comes to Troy.

l: Achaean fleet, The Fall of Troy, BOOK VII
s: The ships shelter the fleeing Argives when Eurypylus routs them, and the Greek defenders hurl darts from the high rampart around them. The ship from Scyros carries Odysseus and Diomede to the island and later bears Achilles' son away toward the war.

l: The Fall of Troy, The Fall of Troy, So came they to the heavy-plunging sea,
s: Neoptolemus sails to Troy with Odysseus, Diomede, and other Achaeans, arriving while Eurypylus and the Trojans are attacking the Achaean defensive wall. Wearing Achilles' armor, Neoptolemus leads a fierce counterattack, kills many Trojans, and forces Eurypylus's host to withdraw. Phoenix recognizes him as the image of Achilles, while the Achaeans honor him with gifts and a feast. Deidameia remains behind grieving as the ship departs, and Neoptolemus later mourns Achilles in his father's tent.

l: Neoptolemus, The Fall of Troy, So came they to the heavy-plunging sea,
s: Neoptolemus sails to Troy and joins the battle when the Trojans and Eurypylus are pressing the Achaeans hard. Wearing Achilles' armor, he fights with extraordinary strength, kills many foes including Celtus and Eubius, and helps save the Achaean ships. The Achaeans honor him with gifts and a feast, while Phoenix and others recognize his likeness to Achilles.

l: Achilles, The Fall of Troy, So came they to the heavy-plunging sea,
s: Achilles is remembered as a mighty warrior whose deeds are recounted to Neoptolemus. He is dead, and Phoenix grieves when Neoptolemus appears as his image. Neoptolemus mourns him in Achilles' tent and longs that Achilles could have seen his son.

l: Deidameia, The Fall of Troy, So came they to the heavy-plunging sea,
s: Deidameia remains in her bower grieving for Neoptolemus as he sails away. She sighs and weeps while watching the ship disappear into the sea-haze, and her mourning continues throughout the day.

l: Odysseus, The Fall of Troy, So came they to the heavy-plunging sea,
s: Odysseus travels with Neoptolemus and helps lead the defense of the Achaean wall. He takes the company to his nearby tent, provides armor, and gives Diomede battle-gear taken from Socus.

l: Diomedes, The Fall of Troy, So came they to the heavy-plunging sea,
s: Diomede travels with Neoptolemus and fights beside Odysseus and the other defenders. Odysseus gives him battle-gear stripped from Socus.

l: Eurypylus, The Fall of Troy, So came they to the heavy-plunging sea,
s: Eurypylus leads the Trojan and Ceteian assault against the Achaean wall and urges his men to continue fighting. He throws a huge stone against the wall and taunts the Achaeans, but Neoptolemus's arrival prevents his victory and forces his host to withdraw somewhat.

l: Phoenix, The Fall of Troy, So came they to the heavy-plunging sea,
s: Phoenix comes to Neoptolemus after the battle and recognizes him as the image of Achilles. He embraces and kisses him, recalls having raised Achilles, mourns Achilles' death, and urges Neoptolemus to avenge his father.

l: Achaeans, The Fall of Troy, So came they to the heavy-plunging sea,
s: The Achaeans are under severe pressure as Eurypylus and the Trojans attack their wall and ships. Neoptolemus's arrival gives them courage, and they fight beside him until the enemy withdraws. They honor Neoptolemus with gold, silver, captives, weapons, clothing, wine, horses, and a feast.

l: Trojans, The Fall of Troy, So came they to the heavy-plunging sea,
s: The Trojans attack the Achaean defensive wall alongside Eurypylus's forces. They recoil when Neoptolemus arrives and kills many of them, though they conceal their fear and continue fighting until night gives them respite.

l: Myrmidons, The Fall of Troy, So came they to the heavy-plunging sea,
s: The Myrmidons rejoice in Neoptolemus as Achilles' son and take pride in his fighting. Phoenix urges him to help the Myrmidons and Greeks in their desperate situation.

l: Troy, The Fall of Troy, So came they to the heavy-plunging sea,
s: Troy is approached by ship after the travelers pass landmarks including Ida, Chrysa, the Sigean strand, and Tenedos. Its walls and the ships gathered along the shore are threatened by the battle between the Trojans and Achaeans.

l: the Achaean defensive wall, The Fall of Troy, So came they to the heavy-plunging sea,
s: The Achaeans built the defensive wall to protect their ships and men. Eurypylus's forces nearly tear it down, and Eurypylus damages it with a huge stone, but Odysseus, Diomede, Leonteus, and Neoptolemus drive the attackers back.

l: the ship, The Fall of Troy, So came they to the heavy-plunging sea,
s: The ship carries Neoptolemus and his companions from the heavy-plunging sea toward Troy under a following wind. It passes landmarks along the coast and reaches the shore near the Achaean ships, where the travelers disembark to join the battle.

l: Achilles' armor, The Fall of Troy, So came they to the heavy-plunging sea,
s: Achilles' armor, made by Hephaestus, fits Neoptolemus closely even though it would have been oversized for another man. Neoptolemus wears the armor, helmet, and great Pelian spear in battle, and the equipment protects him from the many shafts thrown at him.

l: the Trojan War, The Fall of Troy, So came they to the heavy-plunging sea,
s: The Trojan War is shown in its late battles around the Achaean ships and defensive wall. The Achaeans and Trojans fight fiercely, and Neoptolemus enters the conflict to defend the Achaeans and avenge Achilles.

l: the bringing of Achilles' son to Troy, The Fall of Troy, So came they to the heavy-plunging sea,
s: Neoptolemus's arrival at the Achaean camp restores hope to the hard-pressed Greeks. He immediately arms himself, joins the fighting, drives back Eurypylus's forces, and becomes the chief reason the Achaeans survive the day.

l: Achilles' death, The Fall of Troy, So came they to the heavy-plunging sea,
s: Achilles' death is remembered by Phoenix, who says that grief for him continually wastes him away. Neoptolemus is driven to avenge his dead father and later grieves when he sees Achilles' empty tent, armor, weapons, and handmaids.

l: The Fall of Troy, The Fall of Troy, BOOK VIII
s: Neoptolemus leads the Argives into battle, wearing Achilles' armor and driving his father's immortal horses. He kills many Trojans and defeats Eurypylus, the giant son of Telephus, with the Pelian lance. Ares comes to the aid of Troy, but Athena confronts him and Zeus's thunder forces both gods to withdraw. The Argives then drive the Trojans into Troy and begin a fierce assault on its walls, with many killed on both sides.

l: Neoptolemus, The Fall of Troy, BOOK VIII
s: Neoptolemus, Achilles' son, rallies the Myrmidons and leads the Argives into battle wearing Achilles' flashing armor. He kills many warriors, defeats Eurypylus by thrusting the Pelian lance through his throat, and drives the Trojans back into Troy.

l: Eurypylus, The Fall of Troy, BOOK VIII
s: Eurypylus, the son of Telephus, fights fiercely for the Trojans and kills many Achaeans. He challenges Neoptolemus, but Neoptolemus withstands his attack and kills him with the Pelian lance.

l: Achilles, The Fall of Troy, BOOK VIII
s: Achilles' son Neoptolemus wears Achilles' armor and fights so powerfully that the Argives feel Achilles still lives among them. Achilles' immortal horses carry Neoptolemus into battle.

l: Argives, The Fall of Troy, BOOK VIII
s: The Argives arm themselves eagerly, follow Neoptolemus into battle, and kill many Trojans. They drive the Trojans into Troy, surround the city, and assault its gates and walls, though they also suffer many losses.

l: Trojans, The Fall of Troy, BOOK VIII
s: The Trojans fight under Eurypylus and later receive aid from Ares. After Eurypylus falls and Ares withdraws, they retreat into Troy, defend its walls, and kill some of the attacking Greeks.

l: Troy, The Fall of Troy, BOOK VIII
s: Troy becomes the refuge of the fleeing Trojans after the Argives drive them from the plain. Its gates are barred, while the Trojans defend its walls and the Argives attack the gates and the work of the Earth-shaker.

l: Ares, The Fall of Troy, BOOK VIII
s: Ares comes down from heaven to aid the sons of Troy, driving them back into the battle and restoring their courage. He frightens the Greeks, but withdraws to wintry Thrace when Zeus makes his wrath manifest.

l: Athena, The Fall of Troy, BOOK VIII
s: Athena swoops from Olympus to forest-mantled Ida and prepares to fight Ares. Zeus's thunder restrains them both; afterward Athena leaves for hallowed Athens.

l: Fates, The Fall of Troy, BOOK VIII
s: The Fates mock the hopes of Telephus' son before the battle. They determine the deaths and outcomes of the warriors, including Eurypylus' death and the failure of Teucer's arrow to strike Agenor.

l: War, The Fall of Troy, BOOK VIII
s: War is invoked as a force accompanying the battle, with Enyo identified as the sister of War. The fighting continues with weapons, bloodshed, and deaths among both Greeks and Trojans.

l: Pelian lance, The Fall of Troy, BOOK VIII
s: The Pelian lance, carried by Neoptolemus, passes through Eurypylus' throat and kills him. Neoptolemus then tears the lance from Eurypylus' corpse.

l: Eurypylus's death, The Fall of Troy, BOOK VIII
s: Eurypylus's death comes when Neoptolemus' Pelian lance pierces his throat. Blood pours from the wound, his soul leaves his body, and he falls in his clanging armor like a great tree uprooted by Boreas.

l: Greek assault on Troy, The Fall of Troy, BOOK VIII
s: The Greek assault drives the Trojans into Troy, after which the Argives attack the city's gates and walls. They hurl themselves against the gates while arrows, stones, and javelins fall from the defended towers.

l: death, The Fall of Troy, BOOK VIII
s: Death spreads throughout the battle as Greeks and Trojans kill one another. Warriors fall to spears, stones, swords, darts, and arrows, and the plain and walls become stained with blood.

l: The Fall of Troy, The Fall of Troy, Now had the Argives burst the gates, had breached
s: Ganymedes, fearing for Troy and his fatherland, pleads with Zeus, who veils Priam's city and its walls in a vast mist and signals his wrath with thunder and lightning. Neleus' son orders the Argives to withdraw to the ships, warning them of Zeus's power and recalling the destruction once inflicted on the Titans. The Argives bury their dead, wash in the Hellespont, and later praise Achilles' valiant son, while both armies keep watch through the night. Calchas' prophecy that Troy would fall in the tenth year gives the Argives hope of victory despite their retreat.

l: Argives, The Fall of Troy, Now had the Argives burst the gates, had breached
s: The Argives are forced to stop their attack when Zeus protects Troy with mist, thunder, and lightning. They withdraw to the ships, bury their battle-dead, wash away the grime and blood of combat, praise Achilles' valiant son, and keep watch through the night.

l: Ganymedes, The Fall of Troy, Now had the Argives burst the gates, had breached
s: Ganymedes sees Troy threatened from heaven and pleads with Zeus to spare his fatherland or let him be taken far away so that he will not witness its destruction.

l: Zeus, The Fall of Troy, Now had the Argives burst the gates, had breached
s: Zeus responds to Ganymedes by covering Troy and its walls with a vast pall of cloud, drowning the battle in mist, and sending thunder and lightning that frighten the Argives. Neleus' son recalls that Zeus once destroyed the presumptuous Titans with fire and says that all must obey him because he is mightier than gods and men.

l: Troy, The Fall of Troy, Now had the Argives burst the gates, had breached
s: Troy is threatened with destruction by the Argives, but Zeus veils the city and its unscaleable walls so that the attackers cannot see them. The city remains defended for the day, while Calchas' prophecy promises that it will fall in the tenth year.

l: Trojans, The Fall of Troy, Now had the Argives burst the gates, had breached
s: The Trojans are protected from the Argives when Zeus conceals their city in mist. During the night, they watch and sleep by turns in Priam's burg, fearing an Argive assault.

l: the battle, The Fall of Troy, Now had the Argives burst the gates, had breached
s: The battle is halted when Zeus's mist hides Troy and his thunder and lightning terrify the Argives. Many Trojans and Argives have been slain, and the Argives recover and bury their friends before returning to the ships.

l: the mist, The Fall of Troy, Now had the Argives burst the gates, had breached
s: The mist hides Troy and its unscaleable wall from sight and causes the murderous fighting to disappear as though it were a phantom. It does not hide the dead who have fallen around the wall.

l: Zeus's portents, The Fall of Troy, Now had the Argives burst the gates, had breached
s: Zeus's portents consist of the cloud and mist covering Troy, crashing thunder, and flashing lightning. The Argives take these signs as a warning, withdraw from battle, and fear that Zeus's wrath may consume them.

l: Achaean fleet, The Fall of Troy, Now had the Argives burst the gates, had breached
s: The Argives retreat to the ships, remove their battle-gear, and wash in the Hellespont. They sleep in the plain before the ships under changing guards because they fear that Troy or its allies may set the ships on fire and prevent their return home.

l: Nestor, The Fall of Troy, Now had the Argives burst the gates, had breached
s: Neleus' son tells the Argives that their strength is helpless while Zeus protects Troy and urges them to return to the ships. He recalls Zeus's destruction of the Titans, advises obedience to Zeus's signs, and encourages the Argives with the hope that Fate will soon lead them to destroy Troy.

l: Achilles, The Fall of Troy, Now had the Argives burst the gates, had breached
s: Achilles is mentioned as the father whose valiant son receives praise from the Argives. The son later passes into his father's tent and sleeps there.

l: Neoptolemus, The Fall of Troy, Now had the Argives burst the gates, had breached
s: Achilles' valiant son is praised by the Argives as highly as his father during their evening celebration. He feasts in the kings' tents without weariness from battle because Thetis has removed all ache and labor from his limbs, then goes to his father's tent and sleeps.

l: Thetis, The Fall of Troy, Now had the Argives burst the gates, had breached
s: Thetis charms all ache of labor from Achilles' valiant son's limbs, making him unable to feel tired from exertion.

l: Calchas, The Fall of Troy, Now had the Argives burst the gates, had breached
s: Calchas is identified as the prophet whose earlier prophecy is recalled by Neleus' son.
